# Weir v1.0.0-rc.18

Date: 2026-10-14

> **Early days.** Weir is early, and it is in active, hard testing. Expect rough edges. If something is wrong or confusing, please report it on [GitHub issues](https://github.com/jampat000/Weir/issues).

Release candidate 17 passed its full run on a clean machine and was published for Docker, but its Windows release page went up with no files. Releases on this repository are immutable once published, and the old publish step made the release first and attached the files afterwards, so every file was refused. A published release cannot be repaired, so Windows users get the changes of release candidate 17 here. This is the first Windows release since release candidate 13, so it carries everything user-facing from release candidate 17 and from the three release candidates before it: a Windows update that could leave Weir not running, a start-up that watches itself and tries again, a tray that counts its server ready only when that same server says so, how Weir answers a download your media manager sends twice, picking a file back up when it comes back, keeping an imported film from slipping back to "Waiting", a new border on Weir's icon, and no stall on requests on a busy or small machine. Release candidates 14, 15 and 16 were never published. Release candidate 14 was held back because the scenario run on a clean machine found problems in the run itself. Release candidate 15 was held back because that run then found that updating from release candidate 13 could leave Weir not running. Release candidate 16 was held back because that run then found that on a busy machine Weir could freeze for up to 84 seconds on list requests, so a waiting file was judged too early. Everything in all three is here, with the changes for issues #954, #955, #956 and #958, each confirmed on evidence from the clean-machine run.

New since release candidate 17: the release is now published only after every file is attached, a busy database and an unforeseen failure each get a clear answer a media manager can act on, and the tests and shared documents behind them are tightened.

## New Since Release Candidate 17

- **A release can no longer go up without its files.** The release is now made as a draft. Every file is attached to the draft, the draft is checked to hold each one at its size, and only then is it published, in one last step, so the repository's rule against changing a published release can no longer refuse a file. A run that fails part-way leaves a draft, which running it again finishes. A release that is already published is never touched; the run stops and says why, because only a new tag can replace it. Addresses #969.
- **A busy database gets an answer a media manager can act on.** When a write waits for the database for the whole time Weir allows, for example while a backup tool holds it, Weir now answers 503 with a `Retry-After` header and the code `database_busy`, and writes one warning to **System › Logs** with the route and how long it waited. Before, the same moment surfaced as a plain-text 500 that a media manager could not tell from "Weir is broken". `Retry-After` is how long the write really waited, from 1 to 60 seconds. The write was not made, so the same request can be sent again after that time. Addresses #964.
- **An unforeseen failure answers JSON with a code.** A failure Weir did not foresee now answers 500 with a JSON body, a plain `detail` sentence and the code `internal_error`, with nothing of the failure in the body. The details and the stack trace are in Weir's log, as before.
- **New setting `WEIR_SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`.** How long a write waits for the database before it answers 503, from 1 to 120 seconds, 30 unless set. It covers Weir's own writers queueing for the database and then any program outside Weir that holds it. Raising it only makes a media manager wait longer for the same answer. It is listed in `.env.example`.
- **The API reference lists both answers.** `docs-site/docs/api/index.md` has a new Errors table, the OpenAPI description and generated types carry the 503, and the operator messaging standard says an error's wording is never what a client reads: it reads the status and `code`.
- **Tests that judge the thread pool no longer share it with every other test.** A test of the database write gate asked whether the process's thread pool ran a small job within a second, but every test in the same run uses that one pool, so the probe measured the other tests and failed on a busy runner, as it did on release candidate 17's push. The gate test now runs its writers on a thread of its own, with no pool and no clock. A run on four processors showed one other test starving the pool for 10 seconds by waiting on 24 pool threads at once; the tests that hold many threads at once now run on threads of their own, and five full runs after the change had no stall of 2 seconds or more. A switch for the test run, `WEIR_POOL_SAMPLE`, records every wait of half a second or more for the pool, and `scripts/attribute-pool-stalls.mjs` lays those waits beside the tests. This changes nothing in Weir itself.
- **Shared documents from Deluno.** `docs/deluno-weir-contract.md` is new: it lists every reply Weir gives Deluno, with its recording and the test that proves it. `docs/golden-path.md` is updated with the update phase, the keep-seeding group, running a single scenario, the ready checkpoint and the real run times. Both are copies of Deluno's, identical byte for byte.

## The request stall

On the clean-machine run of release candidate 16, Weir froze for up to 84 seconds on list requests, and a file that was waiting for its media manager was judged too early. Release candidate 17 fixed the cause that was found, and added a warning that will record the stall if it ever comes back.

- **The cause.** Release candidate 16 made Weir and its tray look again, up to five times 20 milliseconds apart, at a file that seemed to be damaged or missing. Most of those small files are missing most of the time, for example the update state before the first update step, the update settings and network choice on a fresh install, and a pause request after it is answered. So every read of the update state or settings slept four times on a thread that was also serving requests. Weir's pool of threads starts with one thread per processor and adds another only every half second or so, so on a machine with few processors those sleeping reads used up the threads and unrelated requests had to wait behind them.
- **Missing means missing.** A name that is not there is now the answer at the first look. Weir and its tray replace these files by renaming a new file over the old one, which leaves the name in place: 43,000 renames against three readers at once never showed a missing name. Only a file that is refused (a virus scanner holding it, or a rename in progress) is looked at again.
- **Requests look once.** Everything Weir reads while answering a request or running a timer now looks once and keeps the last good reading: the tray's heartbeat, the update state, the reason an update was held back, the update settings and the network choice. A refused file is answered with that last reading, and the next read looks again. Before any reading exists, the safe side is used as before: update settings notify only, and the network choice is this PC only. Only start-up and the tray's watchers, which have nothing else to do, still wait between looks.
- **A warning when work waits for a thread.** When work waits two seconds or more for a thread, Weir writes a warning to **System › Logs** with the pool's counts (threads, how many it starts at once, work waiting, processors). It repeats every 30 seconds while the wait lasts and writes a line when it ends. It runs on a thread of its own, so a starved pool cannot silence it. A test also keeps the list of places in Weir that sleep short, so a new one cannot slip in unnoticed.
- **Measured before and after.** On a 2-processor server with 24 clients asking at once, release candidate 16 answered the update state with a median of 255 ms, the files list took up to 1,012 ms, and the server handled 923 requests in a minute. With this change the update state's median is 5 ms, the files list takes at most 38 ms and the server handles 2,184 requests in a minute, the same as before release candidate 16 made it look again.
- **What was not shown.** The full 84-second stall seen on the clean machine was not reproduced here. The slowdown above was, and removing its cause brings the measurements back to where they were, but the 84 seconds itself is not proven to have the same cause. If it comes back, the new warning will record it in **System › Logs** with the pool's counts, and the clean-machine run will show it.

## What Changed

- **An update can no longer leave Weir not running.** On the clean-machine run, updating from release candidate 13 once left Weir started but never answering: it wrote nothing to its log, did not listen on its port and did not exit. The cause was found by measurement. If the server's printed output went into a pipe that was full and that nobody was reading, the server waited on that pipe before it wrote its first log line. Weir's console output no longer waits: it goes through a small queue handled on its own thread, and if nothing reads it, lines are dropped and counted instead of stopping the server. `weir.log` always keeps every line. A test starts the real server with a full pipe that nobody reads; it failed before this change and passes now. How that server came to have an unread pipe was not found, which is why the start-up watch below is there as well.
- **Weir's start-up now watches itself and tries again.** The tray starts the server, whether it is the first start, a start after a crash or **Restart Weir**, and watches how far it gets. The server reports each step: starting, opening the database, saving a copy of your data, updating the database, getting ready, starting to listen, ready. A start counts as stuck only when the reports stop for longer than that step allows, so a large database that is still working is left alone and a stuck one is not waited on for long. A stuck server is asked to stop and then ended, and only a server the tray itself started is ever touched. The next try does not begin until the old server is confirmed gone; if one cannot be ended, the tray stops there rather than start a second server beside it, and its log names the process to end. Otherwise the start is tried again after a short, growing wait. The details, and the measurements behind the numbers, are in `docs/start-supervision.md`.
- **The tray counts its server ready only when that same server says so.** The tray asks Weir's `/ready` address whether Weir is up, but that address cannot say which Weir answers. If another Weir already held the port, it answered "ready" while the server the tray had just started was about to fail to take the port and exit, and the tray took that answer for its own server's. The tray now accepts a ready answer only after the server it started has reported that it is ready, either on its standard output or in `startup-progress.json`, in a report that carries that server's own process number. A server that exits instead ends the start as any exit does, and one that never reports is treated like any other silent start.
- **A download sent twice gets the right answer.** When your media manager sends the same download again, the new send takes over Weir's work and is told the result with the cleaned file; the earlier send is told it was replaced. Notes no longer mix, so a film never reads "imported" and "will not import" at once. Answers go only to the connection that sent the download. Addresses #955, #956.
- **A file that comes back is picked up again.** A file Weir saw as gone is looked at again as soon as it is back, instead of waiting ten minutes, and its hand-off is answered. Addresses #956.
- **An imported film stays imported.** A film your media manager imported no longer slips back to "Waiting for your media manager" after its download is cleaned up or handed over again.
- **Two connections sharing a download folder.** A file Weir is already working on for one connection is not taken for another; that connection is told Weir is busy and sends it again later.
- **A new logo border.** The Weir app icon, tray icon, browser icon and docs icon now carry a thin teal border set in from the rounded edge, like Deluno's, and the mark is a little smaller so it clears the border. Addresses #958.

## What You See When A Start Goes Wrong

- While Weir is retrying, the tray icon shows Starting.
- If Weir has not started after 5 tries within 15 minutes, the tray stops trying. The icon turns red and a notice says "Weir didn't start after 5 tries, so it has stopped trying. The details are in the tray log. Click to try again." Clicking the notice, or choosing **Restart Weir**, starts over with a fresh set of tries.
- If Weir was running, stopped and could not be brought back, the notice says it stopped and did not start again after that many tries, with the same way back.
- If the port Weir saved last time cannot be read when it starts (another program has the file for a moment), the tray treats that as a failed try like any other: it waits and tries again with the same growing wait, shows Starting, and never asks for a port or saves one meanwhile. After 5 tries it gives up with the same notice, red icon and Restart Weir.
- If Weir was started by something with nobody at the desktop, such as an installer, the tray exits with code 1 and the reason is in the tray log.
- A server that stopped for a reason that trying again cannot change is not tried again: its settings are not valid, it cannot use its database, or it could not save a copy of your data before updating. Its own words are shown, as before.
- If Weir only started on a retry, it works, and **System › Logs** shows a warning that it needed one.

On Windows, in `C:\ProgramData\Weir`:

- `tray-host.log` says what the tray did: every start attempt with its number, why it failed and how long it waits before the next, and, when a server never answered, a description of the stuck process (how long it ran, its processor time, threads and memory, and the files it had loaded).
- `server-host.log`, next to it, is new. It keeps everything the server printed while it started and anything it wrote to its error output, each line marked with the server's process number. It keeps one earlier file, up to 1 MB each.
- `logs\weir.log` now says Weir is starting before anything that could block, then that it is opening the database, so a start that stops leaves how far it got.
- `startup-progress.json` holds the latest step the server reported.

- **A file that is being replaced is no longer taken for a damaged or missing one.** Weir and its tray pass small files to each other, and each is replaced by renaming a new file over the old. The server could briefly report that the tray had quit, that a downloaded update was gone, or drop a pause or backup request. A reader that is refused now looks again before it says anything, and a file that stays refused is treated as "not yet": it keeps the last thing known, or waits, and changes nothing. A name that is not there is simply not there; see the request stall above.
- **A failed browser test now keeps its evidence.** One end-to-end browser test, `SeededModuleSaveTests.Saved_state_persists_across_settings_and_processing`, failed once in a full run on the way to release candidate 15, and its error was not kept. It did not come back in many later runs, with the order of steps, folder deletes and a fully loaded processor forced, and no fault in Weir was found, so its cause is not proven and it is not set aside. Every browser test now records a trace and its browser and server logs, and a test that fails keeps its full error, the trace, the logs and a screenshot of each page under `artifacts/e2e-failures`. A passing test deletes its own, and the build uploads the folder as `e2e-failure-evidence`, including for a test that passed only on its retry.
- **Every release is proven before it is tagged.** A scenario run on a clean machine — install, update, first visit, real hand-offs from Deluno, pause, Process again, a deleted file and Logs — must pass on the exact commit before any release, release candidates included, can be published. Addresses #954.
- **The scenario run is now done in three steps around Deluno's suite.** First the build is installed over the Weir that Deluno's own installer put there, before Deluno sends any film; then, once Deluno's suite has made its hand-offs, the Deluno scenarios run; then the clean-machine scenarios run on a restored clean checkpoint. Each Deluno hand-off is judged by the Weir that handled it, so a hand-off the previous release answered is counted but never held against the new build. The checks for the update, resent hand-offs, small extras and Deluno's outcome records were corrected against what the first run showed, and a step that goes wrong no longer stops the next one. The run's Logs check also fails when a start needed a retry, unless the run names it.
- **The Docker start-up check no longer ends without a result.** When the container's health address hung, the check could end with no retry and no container log. A hung attempt now counts as a failed attempt, the check tries again, and the container's log is printed if every attempt fails.
- **The contract suite no longer mistakes one server for another.** The suite picks a free port, releases it and starts a server on it. Two starts that picked the same port could both launch; one won and the other exited with "address already in use", but its start-up had already read the winner's "ready" and taken it for its own, so a test ran against another test's server. A server now counts as ready only when its address answers and the process the suite started has logged that it listens on its port. The loser is seen to exit and is started again on a new port. Tests cover a port held by another Weir server and four servers picking one port at once; both failed before the change.
- **A failed contract test keeps the logs of its own servers.** Each server copies its `weir.log`, its standard output and error and its progress file when it stops, into a folder named for the test that used it (`artifacts/contract-failures`). A server shared by the tests of one class is kept under the class name. A passing test deletes its folder, and CI uploads the rest as `contract-failure-evidence-<area>`.
- **One more test no longer assumes a fast machine.** A test of the start-up refusal message read the console before its last line had reached it; on a busy runner it read nothing. It now waits for the line, with a ceiling.
- **The contract suite's record of started servers no longer trips over itself.** The suite keeps one small file per server it starts, in a folder shared by every test class and every run on the machine. Test classes that started or stopped a server at the same moment could collide on those files, and a class that lost a delete left a stale file that made the next run's classes collide again, so some tests failed before they began. Every read and delete now accepts that someone else got there first, and a leftover server is stopped by the one caller that claims it, never twice and never unless the process is the recorded one. New tests plant stale entries and run the callers at once; they failed before the change and pass after it.
- Two tests that measured time against the real clock now use their own clock, so a busy machine no longer fails them; Weir's real time limits were confirmed safe.
- The copyright line now reads "Copyright (C) 2026 jampat000 and the Weir contributors".

## Upgrade Notes

- Windows: **Check now** then **Download update** then **Restart and apply** in System › About, or install `Weir-win-Setup.exe` over the top. Before installing, Weir saves a copy of its data. Two database updates run on first start.
- Anything that starts Weir and then waits for it to answer should allow about three minutes for a Weir that has to retry, and longer for a very large database. A start that goes well still takes a few seconds.
- Docker: change the image to `ghcr.io/jampat000/weir:1.0.0-rc.18`, then `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`.

- **The scenario run is now done in three steps around Deluno's suite.** First the build is installed over the Weir that Deluno's own installer put there, before Deluno sends any film; then, once Deluno's suite has made its hand-offs, the Deluno scenarios run; then the clean-machine scenarios run on a restored clean checkpoint. Each Deluno hand-off is judged by the Weir that handled it, so a hand-off the previous release answered is counted but never held against the new build. The checks for the update, resent hand-offs, small extras and Deluno's outcome records were corrected against what the first run showed, and a step that goes wrong no longer stops the next one. The run's Logs check also fails when a start needed a retry, unless the run names it.
- **The Docker start-up check no longer ends without a result.** When the container's health address hung, the check could end with no retry and no container log. A hung attempt now counts as a failed attempt, the check tries again, and the container's log is printed if every attempt fails.
- **The contract suite no longer mistakes one server for another.** The suite picks a free port, releases it and starts a server on it. Two starts that picked the same port could both launch; one won and the other exited with "address already in use", but its start-up had already read the winner's "ready" and taken it for its own, so a test ran against another test's server. A server now counts as ready only when its address answers and the process the suite started has logged that it listens on its port. The loser is seen to exit and is started again on a new port. Tests cover a port held by another Weir server and four servers picking one port at once; both failed before the change.
- **A failed contract test keeps the logs of its own servers.** Each server copies its `weir.log`, its standard output and error and its progress file when it stops, into a folder named for the test that used it (`artifacts/contract-failures`). A server shared by the tests of one class is kept under the class name. A passing test deletes its folder, and CI uploads the rest as `contract-failure-evidence-<area>`.
- **One more test no longer assumes a fast machine.** A test of the start-up refusal message read the console before its last line had reached it; on a busy runner it read nothing. It now waits for the line, with a ceiling.
- Two tests that measured time against the real clock now use their own clock, so a busy machine no longer fails them; Weir's real time limits were confirmed safe.
- The copyright line now reads "Copyright (C) 2026 jampat000 and the Weir contributors".

## Upgrade Notes

- Windows: **Check now** then **Download update** then **Restart and apply** in System › About, or install `Weir-win-Setup.exe` over the top. Before installing, Weir saves a copy of its data. Two database updates run on first start.
- Anything that starts Weir and then waits for it to answer should allow about three minutes for a Weir that has to retry, and longer for a very large database. A start that goes well still takes a few seconds.
- Docker: change the image to `ghcr.io/jampat000/weir:1.0.0-rc.17`, then `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`.

# Weir v1.0.0-rc.13

Date: 2026-10-10

> **Early days.** Weir is early, and it is in active, hard testing. Expect rough edges. If something is wrong or confusing, please report it on [GitHub issues](https://github.com/jampat000/Weir/issues).

This release candidate lets you check for, download and apply an update from System › About without waiting for the tray, saves a checked copy of Weir's data before every update, and stops a frozen ffmpeg after 10 minutes without progress instead of a flat hour. It also lets a media manager leave files under a workflow's minimum size out of a hand-off.

## What Changed

- **Update from System › About without waiting for the tray.** Addresses #950.
  - **System › About › Updates** now has **Check now**, **Download update** and **Restart and apply**.
  - **Check now** makes the tray look for an update at once, and the page shows the result as it happens.
  - **Download update** works in every update mode, Notify only included, because clicking it is your choice. The page shows "Downloading update..." and then the ready state.
  - **Restart and apply** restarts Weir, installs the downloaded update, and the page reloads by itself.
  - The next step is the blue button. Each button is only available when it applies.
  - When the tray isn't running (Docker, or the tray was quit), the buttons are greyed out with a plain reason beside them.
  - **Download installer** and **Release notes** stay as small links.
- **A checked copy of your data before every update.** Addresses #951.
  - Before installing an update, the tray asks Weir to save a checked copy of its database, settings and keys in the backups folder. The last 5 copies are kept.
  - If the copy can't be made, for example because there isn't enough free space, the update isn't installed. Weir keeps running the old version and says why on About and in the tray.
  - Weir also takes a copy at start-up when it finds its version has changed. That covers installing Setup over the top and Docker image changes.
  - **System › About** shows where the copy was saved.
- **Minimum file size shared with Deluno.**
  - Weir tells Deluno each workflow's minimum file size, so Deluno knows which files Weir will leave alone.
  - When Deluno sends the list of source files to hand off, Weir leaves out files under the minimum. They are never touched and stay where they are for seeding.
  - This needs a Deluno build with Deluno #1199.

## Fixes And Stability

Addresses #948.

- **A frozen ffmpeg is stopped after 10 minutes with no real progress.** It used to run until a flat 1-hour or size-based limit. A big remux on a slow NAS is no longer killed by a flat hour, as long as it keeps moving.
- **An ffmpeg that finishes but won't exit is given a minute.** If its output checks out after that, the clean counts.
- **The same file is no longer processed twice.** A database hiccup could make a job lose its claim and be picked up again. That can't happen now.
- **The tray waits sensibly.**
  - On Quit and on update, the tray gives Weir 45 seconds to stop and shows "Weir - Stopping...", but stays within the installer's time limit.
  - A server that never answers goes red after about a minute. A slow one may take up to 5 minutes.
  - A slow Setup no longer stops Weir coming back.
- A tray test that failed now and then is fixed at the root, so a failed check means something.

The file in your download client's folder, its side files (such as `.nfo`) and its release or season folder all stay where they are, whatever "remove the original after cleaning" says. Your download client and media manager decide when it goes, for example once seeding ends. Only a "Weir only" workflow can still remove its originals.
- **A workflow linked to Deluno is cleaned only when Deluno hands Weir the file.** Weir's own scan of the watched folder no longer picks those files up, so a download is never cleaned twice, and it is never cleaned before Deluno says it's finished.
- **Why:** in 1.0.0-rc.2, saving a Deluno-linked workflow made Weir scan the download folder. It cleaned a film Deluge was still seeding, then removed the torrent's small side files from Deluge's folder. If you run rc.1 or rc.2 with a linked workflow, update now. In your download client, re-check any torrent that lost files, and it fetches them again.

## What Changed

- **Weir sets itself up from Deluno.** When Deluno connects to Weir (Deluno's **Connect Weir**), Weir fills in a workflow for each Deluno library that sends its downloads to Weir, and links it to Deluno:
  - its watched folder is where that library's downloads arrive;
  - its output folder is the processed folder Deluno imports from.

  Weir keeps them in step when they change in Deluno. They show as **From Deluno** in Weir's editor; change them in Deluno. Weir's own work folder stays yours to set (until you do, Weir uses its own temporary folder), as do the rules profile and the schedule. **Unlink** stops the syncing for that workflow. Sonarr, Radarr and "Something else" workflows are set up by hand as before.
- **A refused hand-off says why, and is logged.** When a media manager hands Weir a file that no workflow's watched folder contains, the answer names the workflows Weir checked and the folder each one watches, and says what to set. The refusal is also written to Weir's log, so it shows in **System › Logs**.
- **Older firewall rules are widened once, by themselves.** If you turned on **Devices on my network** under 1.0.0-rc.1, Weir's rule covered Private and Domain networks only. After this update Weir asks Windows once, with the usual administrator prompt, to extend the rule to every network type. It asks only once, and never on a silent or unattended start.
- **The side menu shows just your name.** The line under it, which repeated your role and the computer's name, is gone. The computer's name is on **System › About**.

## Fixes And Stability

- After an update was installed, **System › About** could still offer to restart for that same update. It no longer does.

## Upgrade Notes

- Windows: **Check for updates** in the tray or **System › About**, or install `Weir-win-Setup.exe` over the top. Existing data is kept.
- If you paused Weir because of the seeding problem above, update first, then resume.
- Docker: change the image to `ghcr.io/jampat000/weir:1.0.0-rc.3`, then `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`.

## Docker

- `ghcr.io/jampat000/weir:1.0.0-rc.3`
- Images are published for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`, and run the .NET build of the Weir server.

## Full Changelog

https://github.com/jampat000/Weir/compare/v1.0.0-rc.2...v1.0.0-rc.3

# Weir v1.0.0-rc.2

Date: 2026-10-07

> **Early days.** Weir is early, and it is in active, hard testing. Expect rough edges. If something is wrong or confusing, please report it on [GitHub issues](https://github.com/jampat000/Weir/issues).

This release candidate makes "Devices on my network" work on any network Windows is on, and fixes a misleading message about files waiting to start.

## What Changed

- **Network access works on every network.** On Windows, Weir still answers only on its own PC until you choose **Devices on my network** in **System › About** (or the tray's **Allow other devices on your network...**). When you do, its Windows Firewall rule now covers every network type: Domain, Private and **Public**. Windows marks many home networks Public, and the old rule skipped them, so the page said "Blocked by Windows Firewall" and other devices could not connect however often you tried. Weir is still behind its own sign-in, and first-time setup from another device still needs the one-time setup code.
- **Release candidates are published under their version tag only.** The Docker image for this release is `ghcr.io/jampat000/weir:1.0.0-rc.2`. `latest` stays where rc.1 left it and moves again with 1.0.0. The README, the Docker guides and `compose.yaml` name `1.0.0-rc.2`.

## Fixes And Stability

- **"Waiting for a free slot" is shown only when the slots really are full.** While Weir was scanning a library in the background, a file waiting for its workflow's schedule could be reported as "waiting for a free slot: 1 of 1 in use". Library scans and cleanups have their own slots and never take a file's, and the read-out now counts the same way Weir starts files.

## Upgrade Notes

- Windows: **Check for updates** in the tray or **System › About**, or install `Weir-win-Setup.exe` over the top. Existing data is kept.
- **If you already chose Devices on my network and the page says "Blocked by Windows Firewall":** after updating, press **Try again** on that card. Windows may ask for administrator approval once. Weir then widens its existing rule to cover every network type.
- Docker: change the image to `ghcr.io/jampat000/weir:1.0.0-rc.2`, then `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`. Docker is unaffected by the firewall change: your port mapping decides who can reach Weir.

## Docker

- `ghcr.io/jampat000/weir:1.0.0-rc.2`
- Images are published for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`, and run the .NET build of the Weir server.

## Full Changelog

body:
# Weir v1.0.0-rc.1

Date: 2026-10-06

> **Early days.** Weir is early, and it is in active, hard testing. Expect rough edges. If something is wrong or confusing, please report it on [GitHub issues](https://github.com/jampat000/Weir/issues).

This is the first release of Weir, a pre-release candidate for 1.0.0. Weir keeps the audio and subtitle tracks you choose and drops the rest, for the new downloads that arrive and for the library you already have. It never re-encodes, it works on a copy of each file, and it shows you every file as it moves through.

## What Weir Is

- **You set the rules once.** For example: keep English and Japanese audio, keep English subtitles, drop commentary.
- **Workflows clean new downloads.** A workflow watches a folder, cleans each file that lands there and puts the result in an output folder. You can have as many as you like, each with its own rules and weekly hours.
- **The Library cleans what you already have.** Weir scans it, shows what it would remove and how much space that saves, and changes nothing until you confirm.
- **Nothing is lost if something goes wrong.** Weir works on a copy and only replaces the original once the new file checks out.
- **It works with your media manager.** Deluno hands files over and imports them once they are clean. Sonarr and Radarr import from Weir's output folder, and Weir checks their queues before it touches a file.
- **Everything it needs comes with it,** including ffmpeg and MKVToolNix.

## What You Get

### A look that matches Deluno

- **Weir and Deluno look like one family.** The same deep blue-black surfaces, one blue accent, the same rounded cards, and Inter as the typeface. Dark is the default, and light keeps the same look.
- **A side menu.** It has the Weir mark and groups called Live, Your library, Setup and Weir. Your own name and the version are at the foot, with Change password and Sign out, and the computer Weir runs on is shown under its name. The menu remembers in this browser whether you folded it.
- **A header on every page.** It has the page title, Pause and Resume, and the light and dark switch. A pill appears only when something is wrong: "Paused until ..." (it says how the pause ends) or "Can't reach Weir".
- **Each page's own controls sit on the title line.** Tabs, filters and buttons share the line with the page title. When they do not all fit, the filters fold into a **More** menu instead of scrolling or being cut off. The row of tabs is never squeezed into More.
- **Every page uses cards.** Activity, Library, Setup, System, sign-in, first-run and the dialogs have the same panel look.
- **One set of controls.** Buttons, pickers and fields come in three heights and one style everywhere, and every control lines up with its title.
- **Removing something looks like removing something.** Red is only for removing, overriding or stepping outside normal running: the button that confirms a removal, a restore, signing out other sessions or clearing the log. Cleaning is normal work, so its confirmations are blue.
- **Tables stack on a small screen.** Activity rows take two lines on a phone so file names keep their width, and no table scrolls sideways on a tablet.
- **Each workflow has a colour** from the same six colours Deluno uses, given in the order your workflows are listed in Setup.

### Status colours mean one thing

Every status in Weir has a meaning, and every meaning has one colour, on every page and in both themes. A dot or ring always sits beside words, so colour is never the only signal.

- **Green:** done. Matches rules, Cleaned, Already clean, Finished, Answering, In sync, a backup that worked.
- **Blue:** Weir's own work. A solid dot while it is working (Cleaning, Writing 52%, Analysing, Checking), a hollow ring while it waits or is still to do (Needs cleaning, Queued, Waiting for your media manager).
- **Amber:** needs you. Can't clean yet, On hold, Rejected, a slow connection, warnings.
- **Red:** broken or removed. Couldn't finish, Failed, Not answering, errors, a track that is removed, and the buttons that remove something.
- **Grey:** left alone. Left alone, Skipped, Off, a file in Activity's Kept list, plain information.
- **Gold:** space saved, and only the figure ("1.2 GB saved"). It is a different colour from amber.

Tracks follow the same rule: a kept audio or subtitle track reads green (done) and a removed one red (removed), wherever tracks are shown (a file's story, the Library, Rules' "Try on a file" and a log entry's details).

The Pipeline's five lanes use neutral colours of their own that are never one of these, so a lane is never mistaken for a status.

**Waiting for your media manager.** A file Weir has cleaned that its media manager has not yet taken back reads "Waiting for your media manager". It is Weir's work still to do, not a problem: it is not counted in Needs you, it sits under In progress in Activity, and it sorts with In progress.

### The Dashboard: Live view

The Dashboard is the first page you see. It has two views, **Live** and **System**, next to its title.

- **The Pipeline.** Files move across Incoming, Queued, Analysing, Processing and Delivering as cards, and glide from one stage to the next. A finished file's card says **Delivered** for a moment, then its poster flies to Just finished.
- **Just finished.** A row of posters for what has just been done, each with a coloured status: green for what was done, with the space saved in gold ("1.2 GB saved") or "Already clean" for a file that needed nothing, amber for "Rejected", red for "Couldn't finish". Where there is room, it also says what was removed ("-1 audio / -7 subs") and when. Small windows show a slim colour strip and a short status instead. Chips narrow it to one workflow, and a workflow's tag on a poster opens that workflow in the Library.
- **Today.** What was cleaned, the space saved, and a two-hour chart in the colours Just finished uses. Hover the chart to read a value at any time. It counts whole files and uses the time zone you chose in System › About. It says so when nothing finished in the last two hours.
- **Working on now and Next.** Each file being worked on, with its step and percent, and a countdown to each workflow's next look at its folder, the library clean and the cleanup jobs.
- **Activity.** The latest lines in plain words. It shows only whole lines, says how many more there are, and links to the Activity page.
- **Needs you.** Files that need a person are grouped by what went wrong: not in a language you keep, failed while writing, stuck, skipped by a workflow rule. Each file has its own **Try again**, **Process again** or **Check again**, **Remove...** and **Open**. When nothing needs you it says "All clear". One count of files that need you is used in the side menu, on the Today tile and on the panel, so they always agree. Problems with Weir itself are a separate heading on the panel ("N things to fix in Weir") and are not added into that count.
- **Health.** Each workflow says why it is out of sync, or says plainly that Weir could not verify it. Each media manager and download client shows when it last answered and how fast. **Check now** reads every folder again and tests every connection.
- **Connections light up as Weir talks to them.** A row blinks blue while Weir asks, flashes green when the connection answers and red when it does not, and flashes green when a media manager calls Weir. Nothing flashes while the tab is hidden or when your system asks for less motion.
- **The work switch and the workflow picker.** Everything, New downloads or Library cleaning, and any one workflow, narrow every panel on the page together. Your choice stays in the address, so a link shares it. The picker is hidden when only one workflow is on. On a narrow header the switch becomes a picker.
- **It fills the window.** Live is as tall as your window and shares the height out to its panels. It shows only whole rows and says "and N more", with nothing cut off from 1366 pixels wide up to the largest screens. On a phone the panels stack and the page scrolls.
- **Wording.** Every status on a card is a few plain words, such as "Waiting to settle" or "Can't open it yet". The full sentence is in the card's tooltip, in Activity and in the file's story.

### The Dashboard: System view

- **This Weir.** A ring of how many of Weir's own checks pass, and tiles for the version and update, how long it has been running, how it was started (service, app or Docker), where it listens, how much room its data takes, how many browsers are watching live, how fast it answers, files at once, jobs today, restarts this week, Weir's own use of the computer and the files waiting for a slot.
- **This computer.** Live processor, memory and disk readings drawn as moving traces, with Weir's own share and its tools' share (ffmpeg and mkvmerge) shown apart. A reading Weir cannot get is left blank, never shown as zero.
- **Processing.** How much Weir's work is reading and writing now, and how fast it is going.
- **Storage.** Every drive Weir watches, works on or writes to, with its size, free space, the room Weir's own work files take, the space your workflows want kept free, and a forecast of when it fills.
- **Health.** Every check Weir can make, with problems first, each with **Fix it** and **Check again**. A workflow's whole folder chain opens from **Details**.
- **Connections.** Media managers and download clients grouped with an "N/M OK" count, when each was last checked and a **Test** button on each row, plus **Test all**.
- **Scheduled tasks.** Each workflow's scan and library clean, the cleanup jobs and Weir's own housekeeping, each with when it last ran, how it ended and a countdown to the next. Running tasks come first and blink blue, failed ones show why.
- **Log.** The latest lines of Weir's log. It opens on Problems when today had errors or warnings, and new ones appear at the top as they are logged.
- **Backups and tools.** **Back up now**, when the next backup is due, the newest backups with their sizes, where updating stands, and the ffmpeg and mkvmerge versions.
- **System has its own header.** It covers the whole of Weir and the computer, so the workflow picker only shows on Live. A workflow in the address is kept for when you go back to Live.

### Pages and navigation

- **The side menu is the way between pages; the tabs are the way within one.** Live holds Dashboard and Activity. Your library holds Library. Setup lists its four areas. Weir holds System.
- **Activity is about files.** Its file list shows what Weir did to each one, track by track, and why a file was held or skipped. Its **Needs you** view lists exactly the files the side-menu badge counts, however long ago they stopped, and the badge opens it. **On hold** is its own view. Problems with Weir itself stay on the Dashboard's Needs you panel, and failed jobs are in System › Logs.
- **Setup has four areas, each with tabs** (see Setup below).
- **System has four tabs:** About, Backups, Security and Logs. About is where it opens.
- **System › About, Backups and Security are laid out on a grid** with the controls on one height. Backups is two cards, the schedule and the backups themselves, and Save appears only once something has changed. Security has the sign-in card, the sessions, the protections as a checklist with anything needing attention first, and one Account card for the username and password.
- **A file's story says where the file is now** when it is on the Pipeline.

### Setup

Setup has four areas, each with tabs. The side menu lists the areas, and the tabs are the way around inside one:

- **Workflows:** File paths, Schedule.
- **Connections:** Media managers, Download clients, Alerts.
- **Rules:** Profiles, Playback devices.
- **Performance:** Speed, Cleanup, Weir's timers.

What each holds:

- **File paths shows each folder on its own.** Its table has a column for the folder Weir watches and another for the folder it cleans into, with the end of a long path kept visible. A workflow with no folders says "Cleans in place".
- **Priority is a number you can drag.** Each workflow has a Priority number and a grip: drag it, or use Alt with the up or down arrow, to reorder, and it saves at once. When a file could go to more than one workflow, the higher one takes it.
- **Adding a workflow, media manager, download client or alert opens a panel beside the page**, with its first field ready to type in.
- **Connections are one row each.** A media manager or download client is a name, whether it answers, when it was last checked and its buttons on one line. A missing webhook secret is one warning above the list that names each manager, and an empty list says what the connection is for.
- **The workflow editor folds.** Identity and folders, and the folder chain, are open; media manager, intake rules, file readiness, output safety, capacity, failures, advanced and hours fold away, each showing what it holds. Browse sits beside its folder, and Save stays in view.
- **Rules is Profiles and Playback devices.** Playback devices is one list, a device to a row, with "Built in" for the built-in ones, and Save appears only once something has changed.
- **Speed, Cleanup and Weir's timers are full-width cards,** and Speed shows Save only once something has changed.
- **The time zone is in System › About.** Schedule is each workflow's weekly hours, says which time zone they are read in, and links to About to change it.

### Library: one status for every file

- **Every library file has exactly one status,** and the counts add up to the files: **Needs cleaning**, **Cleaning**, **Matches rules**, **Can't clean yet** (still shared with a download, or unreadable) and **Left alone**. When more than one could apply, Left alone wins, then Cleaning, then Can't clean yet, then Needs cleaning, then Matches rules.
- **Chips across the top** for All and each status show a dot in the status colour and a count, and a status with no files shows a quiet 0. The chosen status goes in the address (`?show=`), so a view can be linked to. What Weir did to a file is a quiet note on its row ("cleaned 2 Oct", or "already clean"), never a status.
- **Why a file needs cleaning.** When Weir can say, a file that needs cleaning shows whether it is new since the last check, was replaced (the file on disk is not the one Weir last saw or cleaned), or its rules changed. The first scan of a library has nothing to compare with, so it gives no reason. Weir never guesses one.
- **One row per film.** A title with several files nests them and folds them, with a summary such as "2 need cleaning" or "5 match". Only a file that needs cleaning can be ticked. The reasons list for files that cannot be cleaned yet sits in the Files card's header while that status is chosen.
- **The header makes room.** The search is a magnifier until you use it, Library setup is a gear, and the workflow picker sits in the Files card. Library opens the library you last picked in this browser when the address names none.
- **Open any file and choose its tracks yourself** when the rules do not fit it.

### Tables you can arrange

- **Drag a column heading to put the columns in the order you want,** or press Alt with the left or right arrow on a heading. Click a heading to sort by it, and click again to reverse. An arrow shows which way. Activity's file list, the Library's files and Logs sort on the server, so the order holds across every page of results, not only the rows on screen.
- **Which tables.** Library, Activity (the files and the Kept list), Logs, Alerts, Cleanup, Weir's timers, Backups, Active sessions, the Dashboard's Scheduled tasks and Rules › Try on a file can be dragged and sorted. **Workflows** and **Choose tracks** let you move columns only, because the order of their rows means something there.
- **Weir remembers each table's order and sort** in this browser. **Columns** on the table's card has **Reset columns**, which puts the columns and the sort back the way they started.

### Logs: one log

- **One list.** Weir's events, its jobs and its server log are one list, newest first by default, under the day each thing happened. Each row says when, how it went (a red, amber, grey or green dot), where it came from (Event, Job or Server), what it is about (Processing, Scans, Cleanup, Library, Connections, Backups, Sign-in, Updates or Weir), the workflow when there is one, and what it was in a line or two. A row opens to everything its source recorded: an event's details, a job's attempts, what it was given and why it stopped (with Cancel pending, Recover result and Open the file in Activity), a server line's logger and exception.
- **Pick one source.** The chips **All**, **Events**, **Jobs** and **Server** choose one source at a time, each with how many rows it holds. The Category, Levels, Workflows and Time pickers then offer only what that source has rows for, and Workflows is hidden for Server, whose lines belong to no workflow.
- **Filters on the header, in the address.** The level picker shows Errors, Warnings and Info, each with its count and colour, and a search narrows the list further. Each applies as you choose it, with no Apply button, and the address holds them all, so a view can be linked to. **Refine** holds what only some rows have: an event's type, result and cause, a job's status, and server lines with a stack trace.
- **Sort it the way you need.** Click a heading to sort by time, level, source, category or workflow, either way. Weir sorts the whole log, not just the rows on screen, and paging stays correct under any sort: no row is repeated or skipped across pages. When the list is not sorted by time, each row shows its day with its time. Drag the headings to arrange the columns; **Columns › Reset columns** puts them back.
- **Log settings** is a button on the Log card. It holds **How long things are kept** (Events and File activity) and **Server diagnostics**.
- **Export** gives the rows the filters show as a spreadsheet or JSON (up to 50,000 rows), and the whole server log as the file it is. **Clear events…** clears the events and finished jobs, and nothing else. It asks you to type RESET.
- **Rows that arrive while you read wait for you.** While a row is open or you are further down, new ones wait behind "N new entries — show".
- **A failed job's next step points at its error** and at Try again in Activity.

### Network access from System › About

- **Choose who can reach Weir from the page.** On the This PC card, an administrator picks **This PC only** or **Devices on my network**. Choosing the network first asks you to confirm, because other devices will be able to reach Weir's sign-in page. Weir on Windows is reachable only from this PC until you do.
- **It says where things stand.** The address another device would type, with a Copy button; "Waiting for approval on" the computer's name while Windows asks; "Restarting Weir" while only the restart is left; or "Blocked by Windows Firewall" with **Try again**. The page checks again every couple of seconds while a change is on its way.
- **On Windows the tray does the work.** It restarts Weir and, when Windows Firewall has no rule for Weir, raises the same Windows administrator prompt as its own menu item, on the PC itself. The rule covers Private and Domain networks only. If you decline the prompt, Weir still restarts for the network, because that is what you chose, and the page shows it as blocked until you try again. A choice already saved when the tray starts never raises the prompt.
- **On Docker and a bare install the page explains what decides it** (the port mapping, the `--host` option) and offers no choice, because Weir cannot change that from inside. Anyone who is not an administrator sees the state only.
- **Every change is written to Activity** as "Network access changed", with the administrator who made it.

### Posters and original languages

- **A poster beside each title.** On the Pipeline, in Just finished, in Activity, on the Library page and at the top of a file's story. Where there is none, you see the title's initials.
- **Where they come from.** Weir looks each title up once through Deluno's metadata service, which needs no account or key, and keeps the poster on this machine. Your browser only ever talks to Weir.
- **What is sent.** Only the title and year read from the file's name, or the ids (TMDb, TheTVDB or IMDb) that Deluno, Radarr or Sonarr gave Weir. Never a file name, a folder or anything about you. At most one lookup a title, spaced out, and Weir waits when the service asks it to.
- **Nothing to set up.** There is no switch for posters and no key to type. To stop Weir contacting the service altogether, an administrator can start it with `WEIR_ARTWORK_GATEWAY_URL=off`: Weir then shows initials everywhere.
- **Original languages come from the same lookup.** Rules that keep a title's original language use the same Deluno metadata service lookup that finds its poster, so one lookup per title serves both, for films and for series. If the service doesn't know a title, the profile's audio preferences choose the tracks.
- **Exact when it can be.** When Radarr or Sonarr report an import of a file Weir handed back, the ids they send give an exact match instead of a guess from the file's name.
- **Tidy.** A poster stays while any file of that title is in Weir. A month after the last one is gone, the poster and its record are deleted.
- **Credits.** **System › About** credits TMDb with its logo and says "TV metadata provided by TheTVDB", both linked.

### For Deluno and other media managers

- **Weir says which version it is.** `GET /api/v1/intake/capabilities` includes Weir's `version`, so Deluno can show it. It is the release number (for example `1.0.0-rc.1`). Treat a missing one as unknown.
- **Deluno can send more about a title.** A hand-off may carry the title, year, TMDb, TheTVDB and IMDb ids, season, episode and a poster address. Weir uses them to find the poster exactly. A field that is wrong is ignored and never fails the hand-off. A poster address is used only when it is on Deluno's metadata service, TMDb, TheTVDB or OMDb over https.
- **Anything else can hand files over** by posting to `/api/v1/intake/webhook/native`.

### Other things you may notice

- **The Jobs table says little.** A queued, running, finished or cancelled job shows one short line. Messages about a real problem say what went wrong.
- **"Already clean"** is how Just finished, Activity and the Today chart describe a file that needed nothing.
- **Messages name the places they mean.** Weir's own sentences point at Setup tabs and at Activity.

## Reliability

- **Cleanup timers and Run now run every time.** Each run lets go of its place when it ends, so the next one starts. Two runs of the same job never overlap.
- **Job wording is plain.** A job that needs nothing from you says so in a few words.
- **Needs you, the Today tile and the side-menu badge show one number.** Needs you reads failed files itself, so a long list on the Live page can't hide any.
- **A library clean stays in Activity** whatever the length of its detail.
- **The System view can't stop Weir.** If reading a drive fails, Weir logs it, tries again at the next reading and keeps the drives it already knew.
- **The log never repeats or skips a row across pages,** whichever way it is sorted, including events stored without a fraction of a second.
- **Saving a Setup tab never wipes a draft** on another part of the page that was not saved yet.

## For anyone using the API

The OpenAPI document (`apps/web/openapi/weir-openapi.json`) describes all of it. The API still says "library" for what the app calls a workflow.

- **System:**
  - `GET /api/v1/system/overview`: the facts System shows about this copy of Weir.
  - `GET /api/v1/system/stats`: the machine's load, memory and drives, with the last ten minutes of readings.
  - `GET /api/v1/system/tasks`: every scheduled task with its last run, last result and next run.
  - `GET /api/v1/system/log`: Weir's events, jobs and server log as one list, filtered by source, level, category, workflow, text and time, sorted, paged by a cursor, with the counts each filter choice would show (`counts.source`, `level`, `category` and `workflow`). `GET /api/v1/system/log/export` gives the same rows as a file. `/activity/recent`, `/processing/jobs/inspection` and `/suite/logs` answer alongside it.
  - `GET` and `PUT /api/v1/suite/network-access`: who can reach Weir, `this_pc_only` or `network`. `PUT` needs an administrator session and the usual CSRF token. Docker and a bare install answer `409` and say what decides there. `GET` also says which way the running server listens, a saved choice it has not caught up with yet, the firewall state, the port, this PC's name and the addresses another device would type.
  - `GET /api/v1/artwork/posters/{poster_id}`: a poster image Weir already holds. It needs the same sign-in as the rest of the API.
- **Sort and paging:**
  - `GET /api/v1/processing/files` (Activity's file list) takes `sort` (`file`, `status` or `when`), `direction` (`asc` or `desc`) and `cursor`, and returns `next_cursor`. A sort, direction or cursor it doesn't understand, or a cursor made for another sort or direction, is refused with `422`.
  - `GET /api/v1/system/log` and its export take `sort` (`time`, `level`, `source`, `category` or `workflow`) and `direction`, and `GET /api/v1/system/log` takes `cursor`.
  - `GET /api/v1/processing/libraries/{library_id}/library-files` takes `status` (`needs_cleaning`, `cleaning`, `matches`, `cant_clean_yet` or `left_alone`), and its `sort` accepts `status`.
- **Fields worth knowing:**
  - `status` and `status_reason` on library files, and `by_status` counts on library totals. The statuses add up to the files.
  - `poster_url` on files, activity events, library files, kept files and the Activity page's cleans. It is null until a poster is found, and always null when an administrator has turned the metadata service off.
  - `last_answer_ms` and `last_used_at` on the media manager and download client lists.
  - `version` on `GET /api/v1/intake/capabilities`.
- **Frames on `GET /api/v1/activity/stream`:**
  - `system.stats`: a reading every second while a browser holds the stream open, and the newest one the moment a stream opens.
  - `system.tasks`: the whole task list each time a task starts or ends.
  - `system.log`: each new warning or error written to Weir's log.
  - `connection.activity`: Weir asking a connection, the connection answering or failing, and a media manager calling Weir.
  - `system.stats` can be the first frame on the stream. Read frames by their name, not their position.
- **Deluno hand-off.** Optional `title`, `year`, `tmdbId`, `tvdbId`, `imdbId`, `season`, `episode` and `posterUrl` are read, and the request is not refused if one is malformed.
- **Setting.** `WEIR_ARTWORK_GATEWAY_URL` points Weir at another metadata service, or `off` for none.
- **Deprecated from the start.** `GET` and `PUT /api/v1/processing/metadata-provider`, and `POST .../test`, answer for clients written against earlier development builds, but there is nothing to set. `GET` always says `provider: "deluno-gateway"`, `base_url: null`, `key_configured: false` and `artwork_enabled: true`; `PUT` accepts the old fields and ignores them; the test asks the metadata service whether it is up.

## Installing

- **Windows:** download `Weir-win-Setup.exe` from this release and run it. You don't need admin rights. Weir asks which port to use the first time it starts; keep 9347 unless something else uses it. If you choose **Devices on my network** from System › About, Windows asks for administrator approval once, at the PC, to allow Weir through the firewall for Private and Domain networks.
- **Docker:** `docker run` or Compose with the image below. Who can reach Weir is decided by your port mapping, and System › About shows that without offering a switch.
- **First run:** open Weir, create your account and follow the setup wizard. The README walks through it.
- **Your Deluno or other media manager:** nothing needs changing there. Deluno can read Weir's version from the intake capabilities.
- **A custom proxy or firewall** that only lets Weir reach certain sites needs to allow Deluno's metadata service, for posters and for original languages.
- **This is a pre-release.** GitHub's "latest release" link does not show it. Find it on the [Releases page](https://github.com/jampat000/Weir/releases).
